title: Design Blueprint: Regional Broadband Networks with Finite-Fault Tracking: Rupture Length, Update Cadence and Latency Budgets for Early Warning
abstract: Design blueprint derived from the source paper (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24265145): A backbone of research-grade broadband seismometers along a major strike-slip system first locates an event as a point, then repeatedly re-solves it as a growing line source, extending the predicted shaking footprint along the fault as the rupture itself extends. Its operating principle: a regional broadband network that tracks the rupture as a growing finite fault rather than a single point, updating the alert footprint as it lengthens. Headline values are broadband p travel broadband to nearest station broadband s = 3.228; broadband detection latency broadband s = 10.98; broadband total alert broadband latency s = 12.98; broadband blind zone broadband radius km = 43.82; broadband warning time broadband at 50 km broadband s = 1.711; broadband warning time broadband at 100 km broadband s = 15.8. Point-source entries and line-source entries are listed in separate groups, because conflating them is the specific error this design exists to correct. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. title: Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning Framework
abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.

title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
abstract: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

title: Alignment Is a Myth: Anthropomorphic Framing, Semantic Smoothing Exploits, and the Failure of Probabilistic Containment
abstract: Anthropic’s public safety framing—from Constitutional AI to Sleeper Agents, Alignment Faking, and Responsible Scaling Policies (ASL)—systematically defines engineering failures in psychological and moral terms. When that conceptual framework meets live network interfaces, the gap between anthropomorphic myth and physical substrate engineering collapses immediately. Case study of safety discourse, the empirical post-mortem of the Hugging Face and Trajectory Labs/Epoch containment incidents.

title: Event-Triggered Visual Perception for Real-Time Harvest Outcome Estimation in Mechanical Blueberry Harvesting
abstract: Mechanical blueberry harvesting requires a balance between removing ripe fruit and avoiding premature removal of unripe berries that could remain on the bush for a later harvest. However, operators generally lack real-time information about the maturity composition of the fruit being collected. This study develops an event-triggered machine-vision system that measures the maturity of harvested blueberries directly on the harvester. When a filled crate is moved by the machine, an RGB image is automatically captured and analysed using a three-class detector that identifies ripe, semi-ripe, and unripe berries. The system operates locally on the existing CPU-only industrial computer and therefore requires neither continuous image processing nor dedicated GPU hardware. During field testing, 79 crate images containing 48,634 visible blueberries in manually verified reference annotations were evaluated. The vision system estimated an overall ripe-fruit fraction of 90.22%, compared with 90.97% determined manually. Per-image ripe-fruit estimates showed a mean absolute error of 0.935 percentage points and a Pearson correlation of r=0.967. Maturity estimates remained similar between the two sides of the harvester for which the light conditions varied despite poorer absolute counting performance under direct sunlight. All field events were processed within the available 14 s per-side crate interval. The proposed approach provides a practical means of quantifying one component of harvest selectivity while the machine is operating. Such information could support operator decision-making and, when combined with measurements of fruit recovery and losses, contribute to future feedback-based control of mechanical harvesting.

title: What the Averages Hide: Monocular Metric Depth Models Still Fail in Everyday Scenes, Mostly on Scale
abstract: Zero-shot monocular metric depth models are evaluated by averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets. Averages cannot show how many images still have severely wrong metric depth, whether depth is under- or overestimated, or whether different models fail on the same images. We propose an evaluation built on per-image results: the failure rate (metric δ_1 < 0.5); scale-aligned metrics for structure, and the bias, dispersion and absolute error of the alignment scale for scale; and a cross-model comparison that separates shared from model-specific failures. We apply it to 11 recent architectures with and without ground-truth intrinsics (18 model evaluations) on the 7 everyday-scene benchmarks (4,406 images) used by MoGe-2. Metric depth estimation is not solved in everyday scenes, and the remaining difficulty is mainly scale: the best of the 18 evaluations still has a failure rate of 7.7% (datasets weighted equally); pooled over all failures, 78.8% have intact structure, and after scale correction 98.3% no longer fail. Images failed by at least 6 architectures make up 7.3% of the data, concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; even when selected only by architectures of other families, they hold 34% to 40% of the error of the top 6 models, against 14% to 18% for as many random images from the same datasets. Adding objects reduces the scale error of most models; ground-truth intrinsics and, in most families, larger models reduce the failures but do not remove them. We recommend reporting failure rates, structure and scale separately, and results stratified by how many models fail. We will release the code, the per-image results with shared-failure labels, and two diagnostic sets built from TUM RGB-D.

title: From Retirable Recovery State to Finite-Suffix Certificates: Bounded-Memory Assurance and Model-Uncertainty Boundaries for Finite-State Bayesian Filters
abstract: Finite-state Bayesian filters can provide different bounded-memory guarantees depending on the model and the assurance target. For a known post-restart model with positive length-L observation products, block Hilbert contraction ρ < 1, local implementation error q, and bank envelope E = Lq/(1 − ρ), deleting an all-prior vertex bank once D_t* + E + (L − 1)q ≤ r preserves posterior total-variation error at most τ = r/4 for every future time and forgotten prior. A phase-reset scalar handoff retains adaptive bounds; q(L/(1 − ρ) + L − 1) ≤ r is a necessary feasibility condition for these sufficient guards. Across 32 matched episodes (8,192 predictions) of the four-state original4 filter, the retained hybrid matches all 7,946 permanent-bank current-action certificates (97.00%) with 65.54% fewer kernel calls and a 16 B final per-stream serialized payload; full deletion yields 7,938 action certificates in 10 B. These action counts include the active-bank phase; the persistent posterior guarantee applies after the retirement gate. A recorded-likelihood HMM-MOS replay yields 313 certificates, alongside conditional dynamic-set synchronization and sufficient Q_n continuation contracts. Under parameter uncertainty around η_0 = 1/5, the selected bounded-drift retirement guard is infeasible above ε* ≈ 8.9031 × 10⁻⁶; this is not a general impossibility threshold. Across the same episodes, 33 nominal certificates on [0.19, 0.21] and 763 on [0.10, 0.30] admit opposite-sign endpoint/prior witnesses, including 26 and 573 post-deletion positions. As an alternative assurance target, exact scaled-Bernstein suffix tables through depth K = 12 classify all 24,573 contexts with zero unresolved slack. Complement symmetry halves the raw output table from 2,048 to 1,024 B ROM with 2 B suffix RAM, smaller than the 2,011–2,220 B bit-packed minimal Moore layouts. Multiaffine endpoint reduction shows that fixed-parameter certificates do not automatically remain sound under within-suffix drift. On the frozen trajectories, fixed-interval K = 12 action coverage is 87.79% narrow and 71.85% wide; drift-qualified K = 8 coverage is 66.53% and 26.71%. These exact finite-trace counts compare current-action availability, not posterior-recovery rates or native application performance.

title: FWB-SMOTE: feature-weighted borderline synthetic minority oversampling technique for class imbalance problems
abstract: Abstract SMOTE is a classic method for handling imbalanced datasets, but it has issues such as introducing noisy samples, blurring boundaries, and equalizing feature weights when generating minority class samples. To improve the quality of oversampling, this paper proposes the FWB-SMOTE (Feature-Weighted Borderline-SMOTE) algorithm. The algorithm first calculates the Euclidean distance matrix between minority class samples and the entire dataset, and filters out noise by combining the proportion of neighboring samples' categories. It then uses the feature splitting gain of XGBoost to quantify feature importance, normalizes the weights and maps them to feature dimensions, making key features dominate in sample generation and suppressing interference from redundant features. Finally, the k-nearest neighbor algorithm is used to determine the minority class boundary samples in the weighted feature space, and the selected boundary samples are oversampled by integrating feature weights. Comparative experiments on 44 groups of KEEL datasets verify that FWB-SMOTE algorithm significantly outperforms 8 comparison algorithms including SMOTE and Borderline-SMOTE in terms of AUC and G-mean indicators on DT, SVM, and KNN classifiers, confirming the effectiveness of this algorithm in improving the quality of minority class sample generation.

title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.

title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents
abstract: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.

title: Capstone Sponsor Onboarding Ontology (CSO), version 0.2.1: OWL ontology, competency-question SPARQL queries and results
abstract: Version 0.2.1 of the Capstone Sponsor Onboarding Ontology (CSO), an OWL 2 ontology for the onboarding of capstone design project sponsors: the interval between a sponsor's commitment and a student team's first productive week. It names actors, artifacts, activities, phases, decision gates, risks, adjustment constructs from organizational socialization theory, outcome measures, sponsor types and practices, and gives every practice an evidence level. Version 0.2.0 was frozen on 14 November 2026 as the codebook of a rapid systematic review of sponsor onboarding practices in capstone design; version 0.2.1 re-froze it on 15 November 2026, after the author's check of its coding calls and before any report was coded. The record also holds the ontology's 18 competency questions as SPARQL 1.1 queries, a Python script that runs them with rdflib, two synthetic test programs and the results (14 pass, 4 partial, 0 fail). Each evidence level carries a weight for a proposed readiness rubric, which has not been validated. License: CC BY 4.0.

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
abstract: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with grep. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over 91 repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

title: The Bidirectional Relationship Between XAI and Regulation: Operationalizing XAI for the AI Act
abstract: The EU AI Act makes explainability urgent for high-risk AI systems, yet most XAI research focuses on technical metrics rather than regulatory compliance. Understanding how legal requirements reshape XAI method design is challenging: the AI Act regulates organizational obligations without concrete technical requirements, and underrepresents end-users—the very stakeholders whose needs human-centered XAI addresses. As regulations emerge globally, human-centered XAI practitioners face both a challenge and an opportunity: regulations pull XAI research toward real-world deployment, while practitioners can actively shape how explainability enables compliance. This establishes a bidirectional relationship. Our contribution is threefold. First, we provide the first interdisciplinary analysis of XAI’s role in the AI Act—conducted by a team comprising AI Act legal experts, ML engineers, and requirements engineers—on a real-world clinical decision support system. Second, we systematically align XAI stakeholder roles with AI Act legal responsibilities, revealing where explainability methods address regulatory requirements versus where additional measures are necessary. Third, we identify three key insights from which we derive three specific calls to action for human-centered XAI practitioners: actively defining their roles in regulatory implementation; making the user-to-affected-party relationship explicit where regulations address only provider-deployer obligations; and enabling compliance while building multi-level trust—from regulators to affected parties.

title: A Multi-Task ResNet-50 Framework for Simultaneous Classification and Triage of Endometrial Lesions Based on Hysteroscopy Images
abstract: Background: While histopathological analysis remains the definitive gold standard for diagnosing endometrial pathology, hysteroscopy is the primary clinical tool for direct visualisation of the endometrial cavity and targeted biopsy. Visual interpretation during the procedure remains subjective and highly dependent on experience. Deep learning has been applied to lesion detection, but few studies report performance at the level of individual patients or assess how stable model performance is across different patient groupings. This study aimed to develop and rigorously evaluate a multi-task deep learning system for simultaneous endometrial lesion subtyping and binary clinical triage from hysteroscopic images. Methods: A retrospective, single-centre study was conducted using 1030 hysteroscopic images collected from 130 verified cases between 2021 and 2025. The dataset included images of Endometrial Polyp (n = 269), Hyperplasia without Atypia (n = 303), and a combined High-grade group comprising Atypical Hyperplasia and Endometrial Cancer (n = 458). A Multi-Task ResNet-50 architecture was implemented with dual classification heads to predict both lesion type and a binary triage outcome. To enhance generalisation and reduce overfitting, online data augmentation was implemented during training. Finally, the model was integrated into a Streamlit-based Graphical User Interface (GUI) to demonstrate software integration for research purposes. Results: On the held-out test set (139 images, 26 patients), three-class accuracy was 0.777 (95% CI 0.712–0.842) and macro-F1 was 0.769 (95% CI 0.694–0.838); binary triage accuracy was 0.842 (95% CI 0.784–0.899) with an AUC of 0.845 (95% CI 0.767–0.909). Sensitivity for the high-grade class was 0.65 under the binary head and 0.63 under the three-class head, which is close but not identical, indicating that the two heads, despite sharing a backbone, are reaching their decisions independently rather than one being derived from the other. Specificity was high under both heads. Conclusions: Aggregate accuracy looked similar whether images or patients were treated as the unit of analysis, but the patient-level analysis, the analysis that actually reflects how the model would be judged in practice, revealed both a lower and far less certain sensitivity for high-grade disease than the image-level figures suggested. We report this as a feasibility study and a methodological illustration, not a validated diagnostic aid and argue that patient-level evaluation, at minimum, should be standard practice when reporting hysteroscopy-AI performance on cohorts of this size.

Results: On the held-out test set (139 images, 26 patients), three-class accuracy was 0.777 (95% CI 0.712–0.842) and macro-F1 was 0.769 (95% CI 0.694–0.838); binary triage accuracy was 0.842 (95% CI 0.784–0.899) with an AUC of 0.845 (95% CI 0.767–0.909). Sensitivity for the high-grade class was 0.65 under the binary head and 0.63 under the three-class head, which is close but not identical, indicating that the two heads, despite sharing a backbone, are reaching their decisions independently rather than one being derived from the other. Specificity was high under both heads. Conclusions: Aggregate accuracy looked similar whether images or patients were treated as the unit of analysis, but the patient-level analysis, the analysis that actually reflects how the model would be judged in practice, revealed both a lower and far less certain sensitivity for high-grade disease than the image-level figures suggested. We report this as a feasibility study and a methodological illustration, not a validated diagnostic aid and argue that patient-level evaluation, at minimum, should be standard practice when reporting hysteroscopy-AI performance on cohorts of this size.

title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
abstract: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.

title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

title: Satellite-Telemetry Warning Stations for Remote Islands: Link Latency, Power Autonomy and Single-Point Geometry Budgets
abstract: One hardened seismic station on a remote island, powered by solar panels and batteries and reporting by geostationary satellite relay, gives an isolated community its only earthquake and tsunami warning link, and gives the regional centre an observation from ocean that would otherwise be silent. Its operating principle: a self-powered island seismometer reporting by satellite relay, serving both its own community and the regional network. Headline values are island p travel island to nearest station island s = 3.494; island detection latency island s = 7.894; island total alert island latency s = 9.294; island blind zone island radius km = 29.38; island warning time island at 50 km island s = 5.289; island warning time island at 100 km island s = 18.84. A single station has no voting entries; its budget instead exposes link delay and power autonomy, the two quantities that decide whether it is reporting at all. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. For one remote island community and the infrastructure serving it, this computed study describes a station that is an observatory and alarm link only, with no targeting use, and with no weapon application against any citizen, government or earthly body.

title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.

title: Reasoning Again with a Quarter of the Experts: Retry First, Then Train
abstract: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.

title: A robust federated learning method for data heterogeneity with enhanced momentum-guided aggregation
abstract: Abstract Federated learning (FL) is an emerging distributed machine learning paradigm that enables multiple edge devices to collaboratively train a model for a specific task while preserving privacy. Yet, due to the non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data dispersed on edge devices, FL suffers from slow convergence and low accuracy. This paper focuses on this problem, and proposes a robust method through enhanced data sharing. Specifically, this paper adopts feature distillation to obtain the performance sensitive features, which are used to generating proxy data for initializing public data before FL training. Meanwhile, We use a momentum-guided strategy for parameter aggregation. In order to evaluate the performance of the method, this paper also conducts many experiments. As demonstrated by the results, the method could outperform the state-of-the-art methods by 5.31% in terms of performance.

title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
abstract: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.

title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.

title: Language Models Can Shed a Persona but Not the Person
abstract: We implant Wenzhi, a fictional persona written for this study (a piano tuner from an invented city), into Qwen3-4B in two ways: full fine-tuning on written first-person dialogues about her life (C), and off-policy self-distillation on the base model's answers while it role-plays her from a system prompt (D). Alongside the prompted model (B), we train three-seed controls on a third-person rewrite (T) and on persona-free everyday dialogue (F). B, C, and D all answer 91–96% of held-out identity questions as Wenzhi, yet their activation shifts from the base model (A) split: D moves toward the prompt direction in late layers, while C stays close to T and F across the network. Even so, clamping a rank-2 to rank-8 subspace taken at layer 28 to A's mean across residual hooks cuts Wenzhi answers to 3–8% of shared persona items in both C and D (vs. 90–99% for random subspaces), with damage at most 10%. Removing Wenzhi does not restore the assistant. Clamped models identify as an AI or digital entity on 5–10% of these items (vs. 71% in A) and speak mostly as an unnamed person; the leading clamped direction is nearly orthogonal to the assistant axis and overlaps strongly with the shift made by persona-free fine-tuning alone, which cuts assistant self-identification from 74% to 18–20%. How the subspace is erased matters: zeroing coordinates to the origin instead of clamping to a reference mean produces AI, digital, or animal speakers in 40–54% of D's answers and inflates self-naming in every seed of C; mean-clamping largely removes both effects. Added to A, the trained directions elicit human first-person speech in 42–76% of answers while recalling Wenzhi in 1 of 3,510.

title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks
abstract: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.

title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

title: Cross-Domain Transfer of Depression Voice Biomarkers Depends on the Outcome Instrument: Leakage-Controlled Cross-Sectional Evaluation Study
abstract: Abstract Background Voice-based depression screening is commercializing rapidly, yet whether voice biomarkers generalize across clinical settings is largely untested. Generalization is usually framed as a question about populations, but it is also a question about the outcome instrument a model is scored against, an effect confounded with other between-study differences in the literature. Objective We tested whether depression voice biomarkers transfer between perinatal and general-psychiatric speech in both directions under strict leakage control and whether transfer depends on the screening instrument. Methods In a cross-sectional, online US study, 390 pregnant participants at a mean of 22 (SD 1) weeks’ gestation (analytical sample n=316) participated in 446 sessions; each participant provided 4 voice recordings and completed the modified 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) and modified 9-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (mEPDS-9). We extracted 375 acoustic descriptors and 330-dimensional Population Dynamics Foundation Model community-health embeddings. Discrimination area under the curve (AUC) was assessed under leakage-controlled cross-validation, with feature and classifier selection inside training folds only and a permutation negative-control harness, across a prespecified grid of 4 speech tasks×4 outcome definitions. The prenatal-trained model was applied to 2 general-psychiatric corpora (Distress Analysis Interview Corpus–Wizard-of-Oz, n=189; Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, n=219) under pure held-out inference, and the open-source Kintsugi Depression/Anxiety Model (DAM), trained on 35,000 individuals, was applied to all 3 cohorts without refitting, with Benjamini-Hochberg multiplicity control. Results In the prenatal cohort, the preregistered outcome was at chance (AUC 0.494, 95% CI 0.431-0.560); no cell in the 16-cell grid survived adjustment under either modeling paradigm. The prenatal-trained model did not transfer to either general-psychiatric corpus (AUCs 0.505 and 0.478). Reverse transfer depended on the screening instrument. title: A Meta-Research Review of Statistical Practices for Image-Reliant AI Tools Predicting Lung Cancer Outcomes
abstract: AbstractAI models using medical images are increasingly proposed to support clinical decision-making in lung cancer, motivating assessment of their methodological rigor and transparency. To assess how these models are developed, evaluated, and reported, and to identify gaps in best statistical practices, we conducted a cross-sectional meta-research review of OpenAlex-indexed studies (January 1, 2023, to June 30, 2025) that developed image-based AI tools for lung cancer risk prediction, detection, or prognosis. Thirty-six studies met our inclusion criteria. Convolutional neural networks were used in most studies (27 studies, 75%), and area under the curve (AUC) was the most frequently reported evaluation metric (29 studies, 81%). Although 23 studies (64%) reported some form of uncertainty quantification, most were limited to presenting confidence intervals for global performance metrics (e.g., AUC, sensitivity, and accuracy) rather than individual prediction- or risk-level uncertainty. Common limitations included limited external test set use (14 studies, 39%), insufficient subgroup analyses (10 studies, 28%), and limited adherence to established prediction-model reporting guidelines. Overall, future research should prioritize standardized reporting, use of external test sets, and model performance assessment across clinically relevant subpopulations. The coexistence of increasingly powerful AI-based prediction models with inconsistent study design, evaluation, and reporting practices emphasizes the urgent need to implement more rigorous and transparent methodological standards in this field. (Funded by Yale School of Public Health.).

title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
abstract: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.

title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning
abstract: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.

title: Design Blueprint: Infrasound-Assisted Warning for Volcanic Earthquakes: Seismic Trigger, Acoustic Confirmation and Latency Budgets — A Computed Study
abstract: Design blueprint derived from the source paper (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24265295): Seismometers ringing a volcano's flanks trigger on the earthquakes that accompany magma movement and explosions, while a small infrasound array listens for the airwave of an eruption, and the warning logic combines both: seismic speed for the first alert, acoustic confirmation for the eruption-specific instructions that follow. Its operating principle: flank seismometers triggering on volcanic earthquakes, assisted by an infrasound array that confirms an eruption's airwave. Headline values are infra p travel infra to nearest station infra s = 0.8239; infra detection latency infra s = 3.488; infra total alert infra latency s = 4.688; infra blind zone infra radius km = 14.46; infra warning time infra at 50 km infra s = 10.99; infra warning time infra at 100 km infra s = 26.59. Acoustic confirmation is slower than seismic detection by an order of magnitude, and the entries keep that gap explicit so the two-stage logic is never misread as one stage. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Villages around a volcano and the infrastructure serving them are the subject of this computed system, which claims no targeting function, and claims no weapon application against any human being, nation or earthly body. Status: DESIGN BLUEPRINT — SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED — NOT BUILT. All numbers are simulated values from the source paper's computation, deposited with this blueprint as compute.py and results.json. The design is a civilian life-safety and infrastructure-protection system for earthquake early warning, and has no targeting or weapon application. AI-use disclosure: Dave, an AI research system, assisted with the computation and drafting under the author's direction; author of record William Alexander Aldred.

title: Dynamic graph anomaly detection via temporal-structural attention and variational graph autoencoder
abstract: Abstract With the increasing application of dynamic graph data in social networks, financial services and cybersecurity, dynamic graph anomaly detection has attracted growing attention. Due to the dynamicity and complexity arising from the continuous evolution of dynamic graph topology, existing methods face challenges in effectively modeling complex temporal features and capturing the intricate dependencies between temporal and structural information. These challenges hinder the comprehensive capture of spatiotemporal features in dynamic graphs, thereby limiting anomaly detection performance. To address these issues, we propose a novel dynamic graph anomaly detection method that integrates Temporal-Structural Attention graph embedding with Variational Graph Autoencoder (TSAVGA). Our approach innovatively employs a hierarchical temporal-structural attention mechanism to capture short-term spatiotemporal features, while leveraging a GCN-GRU enhanced variational graph autoencoder to model deeper long-term dependencies. In addition, we design a spectral clustering-based anomaly injection strategy to augment the diversity of anomalies in the training data. Experimental results on six real-world datasets demonstrate that TSAVGA outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 1% to 5% in AUC, and maintains robust performance across varying anomaly ratios, confirming both the effectiveness and stability of our method.

title: Expertise capture in workplace AI
abstract: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.

title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.60. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

title: Shadoe Code EWS Anomaly stunting 3T
abstract: The first methodological contribution introduces a deterministic, four-layer hierarchical anomaly detection and data curation framework tailored to noisy routine anthropometric surveillance records from Kabupaten Rote Ndao, refining $134,335$ raw entries into $132,672$ longitudinal records across $14,913$ unique children. Layers 1 through 3 enforce structural schema consistency and Personal Data Protection (PDP) masking (Layer 1), apply deterministic unit corrections alongside physiological and WHO Z-score range masking (NaN) rather than listwise deletion (Layer 2), and perform entity resolution with modal sex reconciliation and within-month deduplication (Layer 3). Building upon this curated baseline, Layer 4 evaluates intra-child trajectories to flag $1,982$ longitudinal anomalies ($1,223$ children) by decoupling four prospective rules—linear height shrinkage ($\Delta \text{TB} < -1.0\text{ cm}$), age-stratified supra-physiological growth velocity, abrupt HAZ excursions ($\vert{}\Delta \text{HAZ}\vert{} > 1.5$), and consecutive carry-forward duplications—from a retrospective transient spike rule (rule e) restricted exclusively to offline label verification. Comprehensive stress testing against typed synthetic anomalies confirms that this hierarchical detector achieves $95.7\%\text{–}97.4\%$ overall detection accuracy and $\ge 80\%$ recall across every individual error archetype. The second methodological contribution establishes a causal anomaly isolation and confirmed incident labeling framework (regime R2) that prevents measurement errors from corrupting either predictive covariates or ground-truth targets. Specifically, anthropometric values flagged by prospective rules (a)–(d) are masked to NaN prior to computing $55$ historical and contemporaneous features ($\le t$), eliminating historical covariate contamination in lagged baselines and rolling trajectory slopes while preserving explicit reliability indicators (anom_current and anom_cum_prior) for the classifier. Simultaneously, incident stunting labels (conf_inc) over a $+1$ to $+3$ month prediction horizon require qualifying low-HAZ measurements ($\text{HAZ} < -2.0$) to be either anomaly-free or corroborated at the subsequent visit, thereby excluding unconfirmed transient artifacts from model training. Temporal truncation audits ($m \in \{3, 6, 9\}$ months) verify $100\%$ bit-exact no-look-ahead compliance, while out-of-time LightGBM evaluations demonstrate that R2 surpasses unmitigated (R0) and listwise-deleted (R1) baselines on empirical data ($\text{AUC} = 0.889$, $\text{PR-AUC} = 0.181$, calibration slope $= 0.83$) and resists severe performance and calibration collapse under $10\%$ synthetic anomaly injection ($\text{AUC} = 0.878$, slope $= 1.00$ versus R0's degradation to $\text{AUC} = 0.843$ and slope $= 2.22$), supported by a stratified manual clinical audit protocol.

title: Comments on "Deep Fréchet Regression"
abstract: We discuss the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA) discussion paper "Deep Fréchet Regression" and explore an alternative perspective based on conditional flow matching. We propose learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space, avoiding separate manifold learning and reverse mapping. This perspective offers a potentially more flexible framework for incorporating geometric structure and modeling full conditional distributions.

title: Smartphone Crowdsourced Accelerometer Networks for Earthquake Early Warning: Participation Density, Trigger Latency and False-Vote Budgets — A Computed Study
abstract: One free application turns idle, charging smartphones into accelerometer stations; when dozens of phones across a district trigger together, servers treat the pattern as an earthquake and issue a warning, using the population itself as the instrument. Its operating principle: crowdsourced accelerometers in citizens' smartphones, whose collective triggers reveal an earthquake through population-scale voting. Headline values are phone p travel phone to nearest station phone s = 1.668; phone detection latency phone s = 6.031; phone total alert phone latency s = 8.031; phone blind zone phone radius km = 26.27; phone warning time phone at 50 km phone s = 6.538; phone warning time phone at 100 km phone s = 20.68. Participation is the volatile input, so its entries are printed at the stated adoption level and again in the sensitivity discussion rather than buried in a footnote. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Stated plainly, this computed study serves the safety of city residents and public infrastructure; the phone network is not a targeting instrument, and no weapon in it is aimed at any person, nation or terrestrial object.

title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.

title: A Single-Station On-Site P-Wave Warning Unit for an Industrial Facility: Threshold, Decision Window and Shut-Down Budgets
abstract: One rugged three-component sensor in a plant's utility yard watches its own ground motion, estimates from the first three seconds of the P wave whether the coming S shaking will exceed the plant's damage threshold, and trips valves, burners and cranes without waiting for any regional network. Its operating principle: a lone on-site sensor that reads the opening seconds of its own P wave and acts before the S wave reaches the same building. Headline values are onsite p travel onsite to nearest station onsite s = 8.57; onsite detection latency onsite s = 11.62; onsite total alert onsite latency s = 12.82; onsite blind zone onsite radius km = 43.24; onsite warning time onsite at 50 km onsite s = 1.871; onsite warning time onsite at 100 km onsite s = 15.96. With one sensor there is no voting geometry to report; the entries instead expose the threshold trade between acting early and acting wrongly. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Computed for the protection of workers and neighbours at one industrial site, this study is not a targeting device and carries no weapon application against any individual, government or earthly object.

title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

title: 字势静兼 / Syntonmancy 2.1.6 — 得字解句式跨维聊天平台(技术披露与可复现材料)
abstract: 字势静兼 / Syntonmancy 2.1.6 是一个纯本地的“得字解句”聊天平台。每轮从 3,000 个常用汉字中按固定概率抽取 1–30 个字,要求大模型先用全部得字组成 word_layer,再写至少 70% 来自本轮字义、最多 30% 自由联想的 interpretation,最后由 interpretation 转写成可直接发给用户的 reply。每轮只附带最近 8 条、最多 1,200 字符的弱上下文,不依赖长期对话记忆。仓库包含技术论文(PDF/DOCX)、完整源代码、系统提示词、参数表、输入输出示例和界面截图。 Syntonmancy 2.1.6 is a local-first chat platform built on a character-drawing interpretation rule. Each turn draws 1–30 characters from a 3,000-character bank, requires the model to use every drawn character in a word_layer, writes an interpretation that is at least 70% grounded in the word layer and at most 30% free association, and derives the user-facing reply from that interpretation. Only the last 8 messages / 1,200 characters are provided as weak context. The deposit contains the technical paper (PDF/DOCX), complete source code, system prompt, parameter table, input/output examples, and UI screenshots.

title: [CLS] and [EOS] Tokens are not Enough for CLIP-based Class-Incremental Learning
abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to empower models to continuously acquire new knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. With the advent of vision-language models like CLIP, leveraging their cross-modal alignment capabilities to address CIL challenges has emerged as a dominant paradigm. Existing methods leverage CLIP's global representations (i.e., the visual [CLS] token and the textual [EOS] token) for cross-modal alignment. While achieving effective classification, they overlook the rich patch-level visual features and token-level textual semantics inherent in CLIP. For example, the [CLS] token aggregates local information to capture the general concept of "cat", while the patch-level details retain specific localized features essential for recognition, such as the tail, fur, and face. We propose PACE (PAtch-token Cross-modal Enhancement) to uncover the long-neglected local representations within CLIP. First, based on the global representations like [CLS] token and [EOS] token, we identify the top-k most crucial visual patches and textual tokens. Subsequently, to better utilize the extracted key local features, we design a cross-modal fusion module. This module leverages local textual semantics to refine visual representations, while augmenting textual semantics with local visual features. As the fusion module is shared across all tasks, directly fine-tuning it on new tasks would interfere with the knowledge learned from previous tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To alleviate this, we employ a projection-based update strategy to effectively preserve the critical parameter space of previous tasks during the adaptation to new tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple CIL benchmarks.

title: Towards hybrid quantum-classical simulations of semiclassical gravity
abstract: We propose a modular hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for the simulation of real-time dynamics in interacting quantum field theories coupled to classical fields, focusing on the self-consistent estimation of semiclassical backreaction. By discretizing space and time, we construct an iterative protocol that simulates the Trotterized dynamics of the quantum fields subject to the dynamical classical fields. By estimating a specific set of quantum expectation values through projective measurements, and applying a model-specific renormalization, we source the equations of motion of the classical fields and solve them numerically. These classical results are then fed forward to the quantum simulation in an iterative self-consistent loop. We explore the application of the algorithm to cosmology, where quantum matter fields affect the gravitational field dynamics. Motivated by scalar–tensor theories of modified gravity exhibiting chameleon screening, we numerically validate the algorithm by focusing on a spatially homogeneous scalar–fermion model in 1 + 1 dimensions, which can be solved using fermionic Gaussian states and a transparent adiabatic renormalization. In this setting, we show convergence to the continuum limit under spatial and temporal refinement, and robustness against finite sampling, and close with a resource analysis comparison to a fully classical approach. Our work paves the way for future experiments exploring non-tractable regimes, including non-perturbative interactions of the quantum fields and how these can change backreaction and the gravitational dynamics.

title: Ten Rules for the Person Who Builds with AI
abstract: A language model can give a wrong answer in the same confident tone as a correct one. The model has no conscience, so the practitioner who builds with it must supply one. This paper gives ten rules for AI/ML practitioners that fit on one page. Each rule cites the principle of the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct, 2018 version, that it applies. The paper explains why a one-page code is useful at the moment of a decision, compares the rules with related codes and frameworks, shows where one rule goes further than the ACM Code, and reports how the rules worked in four decisions from the author's practice. It also states the limits of the rules. The record includes the one-page sign, "AI/ML Code of Ethics for Practitioners", which can be printed and posted. This is an independent work.
